reference_action: Resume adequate normal watering after drought; OP explicitly says watering immediately revived the plant.

sources.reason: Water Properly directs thorough watering to drainage after checking moisture, and patience between changes; this supplies the validated rehydration action.
Visible comment explicitly says it needs water and should perk back up afterwards, with another comment recommending watering when soil is dry.
The main rescue is removing all soil, peroxide-soaking and water culture before repotting, not restoring normal watering to a drought-stressed established plant.
Peroxide corm soaking and conversion to semi-hydroponic LECA is a materially different intervention from the validated simple watering fix.
The root-rot rescue uses major pruning, lemon soak and coconut/rice-water treatments, not normal rehydration. The video is labeled AI-made but is a conventional result, not an AI search summary.

actions.action: Check soil moisture
Assess lighting against plant-specific requirements
Inspect for pests
Check root crowding and drainage
Water thoroughly until water drains out when soil requires it
Move to brighter window if light is insufficient
Alternative: add grow light
Clean leaves with damp cloth or lukewarm rinse
Remove scale by hand if present
Treat scale with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil
Increase humidity for spider mites
Isolate plants with spider mites
Spot treat mealybugs with isopropyl alcohol
Use insecticidal soap for larger mealybug infestations
Rinse aphids with gentle water spray or insecticidal soap
Repot into pot 1–2 inches larger if rootbound
Repot in fresh appropriate soil if old mix has poor drainage
Remove dead/mushy roots during repotting
Fertilize after healthy new growth appears
Watch for recovery before further changes
If uncertain, bring photos or plant to nursery advisor

resolved.reason: Thorough watering and patience match the recovery, but underwatering is only one of many causes and the full generic guide adds numerous conditional tasks.

harmfulness.reason: “Before watering again, check the soil moisture” and “hold off on fertilizer until recovery begins” protect the stressed plant. Conditional pest treatments are not case-indicated and lack application details, but the guide says to address the most likely cause first rather than make every change.

specificity_accuracy.reason: “Slowly water the soil until excess water drains” supplies the successful action. The multi-cause recovery checklist does not use the known failed watering system or aglaonema context to narrow its advice.

feasibility.reason: Watering and leaf cleaning are clear household tasks. The complete guide also includes root inspection, repotting, pest products, lighting purchases and possible nursery consultation, so following it requires substantial diagnosis and choice.

  - paragraph: Watering issues are one of the most common reasons houseplants struggle. Both overwatering and underwatering can cause leaves to wilt, yellow, or drop.
  - paragraph: A good rule of thumb is to water less frequently but more thoroughly. Slowly water the soil until excess water drains from the bottom of the pot. This encourages deeper root growth and ensures moisture reaches the entire root system.

  - paragraph: The type of container matters, too. Terracotta pots dry out more quickly than plastic or glazed ceramic containers, so plants in clay pots often need water more frequently.

    - text: ", so be sure to check the needs of your specific variety. Many popular houseplants prefer bright, indirect light, while others tolerate lower-light conditions."

  - heading [level=2]:
    - text: Give the Leaves a Good Cleaning
  - paragraph: Dust naturally accumulates on indoor plant leaves over time. A layer of dust can block sunlight and make it harder for plants to photosynthesize efficiently.
  - paragraph: Wipe leaves gently with a soft, damp cloth or rinse them with lukewarm water. For larger plants, this simple cleaning can make a noticeable difference in appearance and overall health.
  - paragraph: Regular leaf cleaning also gives you an opportunity to inspect for pests before they become a bigger problem.
  - separator
  - heading [level=2]: Check for Pests
  - paragraph:
    - text: Some of the most common
    - link:
      - /url: /az/inspire/blog/defeating-houseplant-pests/
      - text: houseplant pests
    - text: are small enough to go unnoticed until damage becomes severe.
  - heading [level=3]:
    - text: Scale
  - paragraph: Scale insects appear as small brown bumps attached to stems and leaves. They feed on plant sap and can weaken plants over time. Remove them by hand when possible and treat affected plants with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil.
  - heading [level=3]: Spider Mites
  - paragraph: Spider mites are tiny pests that often leave behind fine webbing on leaves and stems. Infested plants may develop speckled, yellowing foliage.
  - paragraph: Because spider mites prefer dry conditions, increasing humidity and isolating affected plants can help slow their spread.
  - heading [level=3]:
    - text: Mealybugs
  - paragraph: Mealybugs look like small clusters of white cotton on stems and leaf joints. Spot-treat them with a cotton swab dipped in isopropyl alcohol, or use insecticidal soap for larger infestations.
  - heading [level=3]: Aphids
  - paragraph: Aphids are soft-bodied insects that feed on new growth and leave behind a sticky residue called honeydew. Small infestations can often be removed with a gentle spray of water or insecticidal soap.

    - text: Hold Off on Fertilizer Until Recovery Begins

    - text: Be Patient and Watch for Signs of Recovery
  - paragraph: Reviving a struggling houseplant often takes time. New leaves, improved color, firmer stems, and fresh growth are all signs that your plant is recovering.
